since 80% of quiz responses are stressing about the menopause belly, we can cater the quiz for weight losing/middle losing

BetterMe's quiz actually is quite good with targetting at weight loss and getting in shape; you can find it here: https://eugenechantk.me/pages/fiftystrong-quiz-question-spec-v2-b8caf878/

can you propose a new rundown of the quiz focusing on weight loss and menopause belly: what are the questions we will ask instead of the original quiz flow? what intersitial we will have instead? what sections will we have in our paywall?
(thinking)
I'll run the session checklist, then read the current quiz flow, the BetterMe spec page, and the research on why women come to the quiz, before drafting the new rundown.

65	**What it's doing:** reflects the chosen goal back as a promise. Establishes the
66	question → validation → question rhythm that runs the whole funnel.

68	### 7 — Q3: Secondary goals
69	**Type:** MULTI select ("Choose all that apply"), checkboxes, gated NEXT STEP button
70	**Options:** Get sculpted and toned body · Increase stamina and endurance · Improve posture and
71	flexibility · Boost sexual drive · None of the above
72	
73	**What it's doing:** first multi-select and first explicit button — friction rises only after
74	commitment is established. "None of the above" prevents a forced false answer. These become the
75	personalised bullet points in the results page later.

77	### 8 — Q4: Current body type
78	**Type:** 4 image cards, single select
79	**Question:** "How would you describe your physical build?"
80	**Options:** Slender · Medium build · Stocky · **Significantly overweight**
81	
82	**What it's doing:** self-reported body classification via pictures rather than numbers — easier to
83	answer than a weight field, and it feeds the before/after visual later. Note the blunt fourth label.
84	
85	### 9 — Q5: Target body type
86	**Type:** 4 image cards, single select
87	**Question:** "What's your body goal?" / sub: "**Visualize your goal to stay motivated and accountable**"
88	**Options:** A few sizes smaller · Athletic · Shredded · Average
89	
90	**What it's doing:** paired with Q4 to create a current→target vector. The subtitle states the
91	psychological mechanism openly. This pair is what powers the "your future body" projection.
92	
93	### 10 — Q6: Peak-fitness recall
94	**Type:** single select, 4 options
95	**Question:** "How long ago were you in the best shape of your life?"
96	**Options:** Less than a year ago · 1 to 2 years ago · More than 3 years ago · Never
97	
98	**What it's doing:** nostalgia/identity anchor — frames the product as *return* to a former self
99	rather than becoming someone new. Powerful for older cohorts. "Never" routes to a different frame.
100	
101	### 11 — Q7: Metabolic self-typing
102	**Type:** single select, 3 options
103	**Question:** "How does your weight typically change?"
104	**Options:** I struggle to gain weight or muscle · I gain and lose weight easily · I gain weight
105	fast but lose it slowly
106	
107	**What it's doing:** lets the user self-assign a "body type" identity (ecto/meso/endo without the
108	jargon). Feeds a pseudo-diagnostic label in the results.
109	
110	### 12 — Pseudo-diagnostic label (interstitial) ⭐ KEY MECHANIC
111	**Copy:** "Looks like you have the **ectomorph body type**" / "You might struggle to gain weight or
112	muscle, but that doesn't mean you can't do it. All you need is the right approach." / "Your plan is
113	designed to help you **get in your best shape without stress.**"
114	
115	**What it's doing:** this is the whole "analysis" promise delivered in miniature, *mid-funnel*, for
116	free. One answer (Q7) is converted into a **named, scientific-sounding category**. It gives the user
117	a labelled identity, validates it, then attaches the product as the remedy. Note the structure:
118	**name the type → normalise the struggle → promise the fix.** No actual analysis occurred.
119	
120	### 13 — Section change → "Activity"
121	The section label in the header switches from "My Profile" to **"Activity"** and the second progress
122	segment begins filling. The funnel is chunked into **4 named sections**, one per progress segment.
123	Chunking makes a long funnel feel finite — you're never "12 of 40", you're "partway through Activity".

125	### 14 — Q8: Push-up capacity
126	**Type:** single select, 4 options
127	**Options:** I can't do push-ups · 1–10 · 11–20 · 20+
128

130	**Type:** single select, 4 options
131	**Options:** I can't do squats · 11–20 · 21–40 · 40+
132	
133	**What Q8–Q9 are doing:** self-reported capability, used to set starting difficulty — and to make
134	the eventual plan feel calibrated. Also quietly establishes a low baseline the product can beat.

137	**Type:** single select, 4 options
138	**Options:** Very flexible · Pretty flexible · Not that good · **I'm not sure**
139	
140	**Note the "I'm not sure" option.** Recurring pattern: every subjective question offers an
141	uncertainty escape. Users are never forced into a false answer, which protects completion rate.
142

144	**Type:** MULTI select, gated NEXT STEP
145	**Options:** Belly · Pecs · Arms · Legs · Back · Full body

148	**Copy:** "Build 6-pack abs and tone your whole body at home" / "Work on your target zones
149	effectively with our Calisthenics Plan and fitness equipment." / "We'll provide **video-guided

157	- **Training frequency:** 1–2 / 3–4 / 5+ times per week
158	- **Workout duration:** 10–15 / 15–20 / 20–25 / 25+ min / **I don't know**
159	- **Sensitivity (multi, image cards):** Sensitive back · Sensitive knees · None of the above
160	  — note how *thin* this is: two options. Their entire injury screen. Our medical screen is a
161	  genuine differentiator.
162	- **Conditional reassurance:** "We got you!" → "You'll find lots of exercises that also strengthen
163	  your back." Fired by the back selection.
164	- **Equipment experience:** Yes and I loved it / Yes but it didn't work for me / No, never tried it

166	### 23 — Section change → "Lifestyle & Habits" · objection mining ⭐
167	**Question:** "Why haven't you tried using fitness equipment before?" (7 options, two columns)
168	It appears challenging · I lack the equipment · **It seems pricey** · I'm uncertain about its
169	effectiveness · I'm worried about proper usage · I prefer bodyweight exercises · Other
170	
171	**Selected "It seems pricey" → immediately served:** *"Gear on a budget — **Unlock a special
172	discount** to build a lean, muscular body without overspending. No need for personal coaches or
173	pricey gym memberships."*
174	
175	**What it's doing:** this is not a profiling question, it is **objection harvesting**. The answer
176	selects a matched rebuttal, and the price objection specifically pre-loads a discount promise that
177	is redeemed 15 steps later at the scratch card. Objection → rebuttal → deferred payoff.
178	
179	### 24–30 — Lifestyle battery
180	- **Work schedule** (icons): 9 to 5 · Night shifts · Flexible · **I'm retired/not working right now**
181	  — the option set is **age-conditional**; "retired" appears because 50+ was selected.
182	- **Typical day:** Mostly sitting · On my feet · Balance · Changes daily
183	- **Energy levels:** Low and inconsistent · **Crash by midday** · Steady with minor dips · High all day
184	  → reassurance: *"Beat the afternoon slump for good"*
185	- **Water intake** (with unit explainer: "1 average glass is 8 oz or 237 ml")
186	- **Habits (multi):** Emotional or boredom eating · Overeating · Late-night snacking · Skipping meals
187	- **Diet type:** grouped single-select with category headers (WITH MEAT / WITHOUT MEAT / WITH FISH /
188	  WITHOUT ALLERGENS) and a descriptive subtitle per option. New question archetype.
189	  → **product preview interstitial**: "Your Meals" card showing Breakfast 517 kcal · 8 min,
190	  Lunch 597 kcal · 20 min, Dinner 601 kcal · 25 min. Seeds the meal-plan upsell by *showing* it.
191	
192	### 31–32 — Health-data consent gate ⭐
193	**"Do you smoke?"** and **"How often do you drink alcohol?"** each carry:
194	- an explicit checkbox — *"I consent to BetterMe processing my health onboarding data to provide
195	  services and enhance my user experience. Privacy Policy"*
196	- a **SKIP THIS QUESTION** link
197	
198	**What it's doing:** special-category health data under GDPR needs explicit consent. They attach it
199	to the first genuinely medical questions and make those questions skippable. By the height screen
200	the consent becomes **mandatory** — attempting to continue without it throws *"Consent required to
201	continue"*. Directly relevant: our entire quiz is health data.
202	
203	### 33–36 — Section change → "Weight Goals" · numeric inputs
204	Height (ft/cm toggle, range validation 90–243 cm) → current weight (lbs/kg, 25–300 kg) → goal
205	weight → **exact age**. Free-text numeric entry is the highest-friction input type and it lands
206	**last**, in section 4 of 4. Exact age is asked here despite the age *band* being step 1.
207	
208	### 37 — "Analyzing your answers…" ⭐ processing theatre
209	Four progress bars, **one per quiz section** — Your Profile, Activity, Lifestyle & Habits, Weight
210	Goals — filling sequentially with a checkmark on completion. Takes **~3 minutes**, deliberately.
211	Apple "App of the Day (160 countries)" and Trustpilot "Excellent" badges rotate underneath.
212	
213	**What it's doing:** manufacturing perceived computational effort. The four bars map onto the four
214	sections you answered, so the wait *feels* like your specific answers being processed. The award
215	badges convert dead time into trust-building.

217	### 38 — "Here's your wellness profile" ⭐⭐ THE ANALYSIS
218	| Element | Content |
219	|---|---|
220	| **BMI gauge** | "You – 26.99" on a 15→40 scale, bands UNDERWEIGHT / NORMAL / **OVERWEIGHT** / OBESE |
221	| **Red risk panel** | "Risks of unhealthy BMI: High blood pressure, increased risk of heart attack, stroke, type 2 diabetes, chronic back and joint pain" |
222	| Lifestyle | Sedentary |
223	| Fitness level | **Advanced** |
224	| Metabolism | Fast, difficult to gain muscle |
225	| Visual | Rendered 3D body model, visibly overweight |
226	
227	**Two things worth noting.**
228	
229	1. **It contradicts its own inputs.** I answered *1–10 push-ups*, *11–20 squats*, and flexibility
230	   *"not that good"* — and it returned **Fitness level: Advanced**. This is direct evidence that the
231	   "analysis" is substantially decorative. BMI is the only genuinely computed number
232	   (170 cm / 78 kg = 26.99 ✓), and BMI is a discredited individual health measure, especially
233	   after 50 where it ignores body composition entirely.
234	2. **The risk panel is a fear lever**, not information. Heart attack and stroke, in red, immediately
235	   before the offer.

=== ISSUE FUNNELS ===
# Issue funnels — before/after in the "Says Who" format

2026-09-03 · Sources: `.claude/quiz-research/menopause-health-research.html` (clinical prevalence),
`.claude/research-influencer/insights.html`, `ads/competitor-menopause/SWIPE.md`,
`.claude/ads-research/dissection-a-says-who-age-variants.md` (the format), and a fresh PostHog
tally of `quiz_screen_submitted` (last 60 days, ~500 quiz respondents).

## 1. Which issues — research vs what our own quiz-takers say

| Issue | Clinical prevalence (research page) | Our quiz (n≈420–500) | Honest claim strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Menopause belly / shape change | visceral fat 5–8% → 15–20% of body fat | **80% pick it as THE goal** (s1-4); 65% tick "shape changed around the middle" | Do-not-claim as weight loss. Claim body composition/strength; show, don't say |
| Lower back | part of the 70%+ musculoskeletal syndrome | **56% stiff/achy in lower back** (top location); 25% list back/neck as a condition to work around | Claim carefully: less stiffness, moving without thinking |
| Knees + hips / getting off the floor | 25% disabled by MSK symptoms; 40% clean scans | knees 47%, hips 41%; **51% can't get up from the floor without a hand** | Strong: floor-transfer + sit-to-stand ladder is literally the programme |
| Balance / steadiness | falls −35–40% (Otago) | 22% "less steady"; 28% can't hold one leg 10s; only 3% make it their goal | **Strongest honest claim we have** |
| Sleep / energy | 40–69% disturbed sleep | 58% / 54% | Not visualisable as before/after; use as after-context |
| Leaking | 44–57% | 76% at least "once in a while" | Real, huge, but not a public before/after format |
| Hot flushes | >50% persist | 26% | Do not claim |

Caveat: these respondents were recruited by the body-transformation "Says Who" ad, which inflates the
weight-loss goal. It is still the dominant felt problem by a mile. Balance is the reverse case: lowest
felt demand, strongest evidence — the research says it should anchor the product, the quiz says almost
nobody arrives asking for it.

## 2. What is frozen (the four load-bearing elements)

From the dissection: quoted dismissal caption on 100% of the before → genuinely unflattering before
(46% of runtime) → strobe resolving on the 6.82s drop → `says who?` from the resolve to the end. Three
after-contexts (home / outdoor / car), same track, same cut list, hair colour and identity survive,
after reads ~a decade younger (Eugene's dramatic-delta call). Only the dismissal line, the before
*action*, and the after *actions* turn per issue.

The change from the age variants: the before no longer shows "old"; it shows **the problem being
done** — a physical action she recognises. The after shows the same action done easily, then the life
that follows.

## 3. The four storyboards

### A · Menopause belly — recommended first (demand)
- Hook: `"it's menopause belly / nothing you can do"` · backup `"after 50 / the middle just spreads"`
- Before (bathroom, cold light): tugging the tee down over the belly → jeans that won't button, pinch the roll → profile, hands under the lower belly. 
- Strobe pair: before profile hands-on-belly ⇄ after profile hands on waist, same head scale.
- After 1 (bedroom): fitted tank + high-waist leggings, arms stretch overhead, grin. After 2: park run. After 3: car.
- Copy: "Nothing works after 50." It isn't true. Your body changed the rules, not the other way round … at 48, at 55, at 62. Fifteen minutes, three days a week, at home.
- Guardrails: never a number, scale, tape, or the words lose/fat/inches in caption or copy. The shipped winner already does the stomach pinch and cleared review; keep the claim in the dismissal, not in a promise.

### B · Lower back
- Hook: `"it's your age / your back will always hurt"` · backup `"bad back at 58? / learn to live with it"`
- Before (bedroom, morning, cold light): sat on the edge of the bed, hand pressed to the lower back → tries to stand, stalls bent at the hip → straightens in stages, hand on the hip.
- Strobe pair: seated edge-of-bed before ⇄ seated edge-of-bed after, upright; the after then stands in one movement.
- After 1: same room, picks the laundry basket up off the floor and swings it onto a hip. After 2: park, bends to tie a shoe mid-walk / lifts a grandchild. After 3: car, twists easily to grab the seatbelt.
- Funnel line (intro): "The scan can be clean and the pain still real." 40% of scans are normal.
- Guardrails: no "pain-free", no "fix your back". Claim "move without thinking about it".

### C · Knees, hips, the floor
- Hook: `"at your age / stay off the floor"` · backup `"bad knees? / that's just 60"`
- Before (living room carpet): on the floor with a grandchild's toy/dog → hands on the coffee table hauling up → halfway, hand on the knee, wince.
- Strobe pair: sat on the floor before ⇄ sat on the floor after, cross-legged and upright; the after rises without hands.
- After 1: same carpet, up in one movement, laughs. After 2: park, hiking steps briskly. After 3: car.
- Guardrails: keep the floor-rise as the proof, not a knee "cure".

### D · Balance — recommended for the 60s+ cell
- Hook: `"you're 63 / be careful now"` · backup `"at your age / hold the rail"`
- Before (hallway/front door): bends to put on a shoe standing → wobbles → grabs the doorframe, hand to chest.
- Strobe pair: standing at the doorframe before (hand on frame) ⇄ standing in the same doorway after, one foot lifted, no hands.
- After 1: shoe goes on one-legged, no hands, grin. After 2: park/beach, brisk walk, steps without the rail. After 3: car.
- Copy: "Be careful" is the thing that speeds it up. A home balance programme cuts falls by a third. At home, no equipment.
- Note: at 63+ the after is strong-not-sculpted (dissection's V60 rule), still ~a decade younger.

## 4. Funnel wiring
- Phase 1: four ads in one campaign, same quiz, `utm_content=issue-belly|back|floor|balance`. Nothing on the quiz changes.
- Phase 2 (for any cell that wins): issue-matched intro line on `s0-1` and preselect the matching `s1-4` goal; interstitials already exist for stiffness, balance, and the "clean scan".
- Decision rule: run each to ~50 leads; compare CPL vs the A56 control first, checkout rate second; kill at CPL +50%; swap the backup line before abandoning an issue.

## 5. Recommended order
1. Belly (80% demand) with policy guardrails
2. Back (56%; the "clean scan" line is the best interstitial we have)
3. Floor (51% functional failure; cheapest honest proof)
4. Balance, aimed at 60+ (strongest claim, lowest felt demand)

## 6. Production
Same pipeline as V40: after sheet → derived before sheet → strobe-pair frames → alpha-blend gate (6cr de-risk) → clips via minimax_h3 → existing ffmpeg cut list and audio bed. Per variant ~250–350cr. Before-clip traps from V40 apply: force the body at the scene-frame level, expect a re-roll on the before. Nothing generates until approved.

## 7. Extra physical symptoms from the Reddit / forum corpus (added 2026-09-03)

Sources: `deep-research/runs/menopause-mobility-evidence-20260813-082503/angle-6-lived-experience.md`
(6,251 Reddit posts, 31 threads read), `deep-research/runs/menopause-women-desires-20260829-064404/`
(316 threads + 1,080 YouTube comments), synthesised in `.claude/audience-research/brief.html`.

| Symptom (her words) | Corpus signal | Quiz signal | Before/after potential | Claim |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **After-sitting stiffness** — "I get up like I'm 95", "Tin Man", "worse after sitting or driving" | Very widely repeated; felt as surprising | (not asked) | **Best new before beat.** Getting off the couch / out of the car in stages. Upgrades the back and floor befores; the car after-context becomes proof | Mobility, claim carefully |
| **Hands** — "finger joints so swollen I can't wear rings", "got my thumbs back and could open jars" | Named first in the joint list | 16% | Jar lid: cheapest, most recognisable before/after in the set | Grip strength only; joint pain is HRT territory in her mind |
| **Frozen shoulder** — "the first sign" | Widely described | 39% shoulders/neck | Reaching the top shelf, coat, bra strap, hair | Amber: evidence says peri vs pre not significant; PT strengthening made it worse for some |
| **Stairs** — knee pain going down, "out of breath going up", "climb stairs without being out of breath" (GenXWomen) | Early, specific pain signal | 43% puffed at the top | Hand on the rail, one step at a time → two at a time. Fits floor or balance | Strong: loaded stair climb is the programme's retest |
| **Feet/ankles first thing** — "my ankles are toast", plantar fascia, Achilles | Common | 30% | Hobbling first steps out of bed; a before beat, not a funnel | Weak |
| **Night pain** — 3am hips "crushed in a vice" | Common | sleep 58% | Not visual | None |
| **Elbows** — "sudden onset tennis elbow, both arms" | Surprisingly often | — | Skip | None |
| **Deep squat / floor gone** — "haven't touched the floor for five years", "avoid sitting because it's so hard to get back up" | Flagship functional fear | 51% | Reinforces funnel C; "five years" is a hook line | Strong |
| **Where the weight lands** — "Christmas hams down the back of my pants", "lost my edges", "deflated balloon" | 12+ threads | 65% | Vocabulary for funnel A, not a new funnel | Do not claim |
| **Brain fog** — "losing my mind" | ≥14 threads, rivals body distress | (not asked) | Not a physical before/after; the whitespace is a separate test | Amber wording only |

Three warnings the corpus adds to the storyboards:
1. **Joint-pain relief is HRT's claim in her mind** ("estrogen was the only thing that helped my joints"; "exercise only increased my joint pain"). Back, hands and shoulder funnels promise moving easily, never pain relief.
2. **Her proof grammar**: same outfit, pose and place; big deltas read as fake or Ozempic post-2024; "I hate being shown before/after pics to sell me something". This cuts against the dramatic-delta rule. The shipped A56 numbers are the only real data, so keep the rule, but it argues for the *action* delta (gets up, reaches, opens the jar) carrying more of the load than the body delta.
3. **Meta bans weight-loss before/after imagery outright** and the ASA banned a 12-week menopause programme for the belly claims. Funnel A is the highest-rejection-risk cell; the action-based befores (car, couch, jar, shelf) are safer on both counts.

Recommended additions: fold **after-sitting stiffness** into B and C as the first before beat; add a fifth candidate, **E · Hands (the jar)**, cheap enough to test alongside; use stairs as After 2 for C and D.

## 8. What quiz-takers actually want (PostHog, per-person crosstab, 60 days, n=473 with a goal)

**The goal is one thing; the problem is a stack.**

- 82% pick "lose weight, especially around my middle" as their one goal. It holds at every age (63% at 45–49 on n=19, 87% at 50–54, 79% at 55–59, 90% at 60–64, 79% at 65+) and every stage (63% peri, 80% menopause, 73% post, 66% unsure).
- The women who pick weight carry the same symptom stack as the women who don't: stiff 48% vs 52%, energy dips 55% vs 56%, broken sleep 59% vs 59%, things heavier 33% vs 32%. Average 3.1 symptoms ticked in both groups. Only "shape changed" separates them (69% vs 49%).
- Functionally they are the same women: 47% cannot get off the floor unaided, 57% stiff in the lower back, 45% knees, 75% leak at least sometimes, 52% find stairs hard, 88% sleep badly, 23% crash by mid-afternoon.
- The one discriminator is balance: the non-weight group is twice as likely to feel unsteady (38% vs 19%) and to fail the one-leg test (54% vs 33%).
- Why it matters to her (multi-select): feel better in myself 82%, stay independent 72%, heart and bones 70%, not needing looking after 58%, family 55%.

Read: the middle is the ticket she buys with, not the problem she lives with. The goal question forces one answer, the weight option sits first and is the only appearance option, and this sample was recruited by a body-transformation ad, so 82% overstates it. But even at a discount it is the door. For the funnels: the dismissal in the hook can name the middle, but the before beats should show the stack she actually has (couch, floor, stairs, back, tired by 3pm) and the after must show ease and energy, not a smaller body. Worth testing in the quiz: rotate the goal options, or add "and what else?" as a second pick.

## 9. Position: focus on the middle, not on weight (2026-09-03, pending Eugene's call)

**The leak.** 82% pick the middle as their goal; the result screen then says "Balance is where you have the most to gain", the plan blocks are hips/back/floor, and the paywall testimonials are the banister, the sneeze, the floor and the afternoon slump. Nothing between the goal question and the pay button answers what she came for. Fix this before any new ad; it applies to every ad.

**Why the middle rather than weight loss**
- Science delivers the middle, not the scale: visceral fat ~−6% with zero weight loss; 12-week home RCT waist −1.4 cm vs controls +2.0 cm; scale −0.5 to −2 kg only.
- Her words already separate them: "it's not the weight gain, it's WHERE I'm gaining it".
- Compliance: Meta bans weight-loss before/after imagery; ASA banned Sculpted Vegan's 12-week menopause programme for "rapid fat loss". Green: "exercise targets deep belly fat even when the scale barely moves". Red: "lose belly fat in 12 weeks".
- Reverse Health's longest-running ads sell inches, bloating, energy, never pounds.
- Believability: silhouette change at 12 weeks reads fake ("3 months ain't jack"); firmness, clothes fit, waist number are believed.

**Mindful of her body, concretely**
- Claims: measurably stronger, firmer through the middle, clothes fit differently, energy by week 4. Never pounds, never a numbered timeframe, never the scale.
- Hook = mechanism in her words: the body changed the rules; oestrogen moved fat from under the skin to around the organs; what used to work stopped working.
- Proof: her own waist measure week 1 vs 12, process receipts, modest age-stated results.
- Creative: Says Who already shows the middle without saying it. After = upright, firm, energetic, not thin.

**Order of changes**
1. Result screen + paywall answer the chosen goal. For the 82%: outlook leads with the middle ("deep belly fat is the most reversible thing on your list, and it moves before the scale does"); one testimonial about jeans.
2. Belly funnel becomes the lead creative; other issues become its before beats and after contexts.
3. Test the goal question (option order; second pick).

**Caveat:** the programme is strength/balance/mobility at 15 min × 3. That yields the modest visceral/waist changes above. If the middle is the front door, the plan owes her a visible walking/conditioning strand, not an implied one.

## AGENT B — UK ASA / META / FTC COMPLIANCE SURFACE

### Controlling precedent — direct analog
**Kim Constable t/a The Sculpted Vegan (ASA A22-1153813, 5 Oct 2022)**: a 12-week menopause fitness/diet program's Meta ads banned. Banned claims: "12 weeks to Rapid Fat Loss in Menopause"; "most women easily lose 5% of their body fat in the first 14 days"; "drop up to 40 pounds of fat in just 12 weeks"; "reduce hot flashes by 50%"; "I've hacked the precise science of fitness for menopausal women." Rules breached: 3.1, 3.7, 12.1 (health claims need trials on menopausal women), 12.2 (discouraging medical treatment), 13.9. Hundreds of testimonials + before/afters REJECTED as substantiation. Holding: a fitness program claiming to treat menopause symptoms ("helps hot flashes", "reduces brain fog") IS making a health/treatment claim requiring clinical evidence — effectively prohibited.

### Menopause ruling wave
ASA runs AI-driven monitoring hunting menopause claims (2024, 2025–26 sweeps). Happy Koala/MenoDaily (Jul 2024): "Day 1: Zero brain fog… Day 7: no hot flashes… lost 8kgs" banned — brain fog, hot flashes, sleep, mood, bloating each ruled menopause symptom/disease claims; even the product NAME can imply treatment. Also: Femgroup ("95% Success Rate"), Dr Vegan (HRT equivalence), Nova, Lunera, Minerva (Mar 2026).

### CAP Code rules binding a fitness program
- 13.1: efficacy claims need rigorous trials on people; testimonials never substitute.
- 13.2: cannot target/depict the obese unless program meets 5 criteria (12-month efficacy etc.) — use overweight-at-most imagery.
- 13.9: NO precise weight-loss amount in a stated period for prospective users ("lose 10 lbs in 4 weeks" banned regardless of evidence).
- 13.10: implied rate must not exceed 2 lbs/week.
- Testimonials (3.45–3.50): genuine, signed, dated proof; an individual's "I lost 8 lbs in six weeks" OK only if documented, ≤2 lbs/week, AND general efficacy independently substantiated; must never imply others could lose a specific amount in stated time.
- Before/afters: signed/dated proof, unmanipulated (retain originals), representative of typical results; disclaimers can't cure a misleading image.
- Guarantees (3.53–3.55): state limitations pre-purchase; promptly refund; guarantee satisfaction/refund, not outcomes.

### Meta policy layer (US + UK)
- Personal attributes: copy must not assert/imply knowledge of personal characteristics — "you're over 50", "are you going through menopause" are violations; use third person ("for women over 50"). 2026 enforcement flags implied attribution and scans landing pages.
- **Meta prohibits weight-loss before/after imagery outright** (stricter than ASA) — removes before/afters from Meta creative pool in both markets.
- No idealized/negative body-image content; no guaranteed results; 18+ targeting for weight loss.

### US side
FTC: "competent and reliable scientific evidence"; testimonials must reflect TYPICAL results (no "results not typical" safe harbor). Net: copy written to ASA standard is simultaneously US-safe; FTC adds only typicality on testimonials.

Allowed (low risk): "Strength training designed for women over 50"; generic NHS-consistent benefits (strength, energy, mobility, bone health, mood — unquantified, not treatment-framed); menopause education without treatment implication; structural facts (12-week, at-home); documented individual result within limits; satisfaction guarantee honored promptly.
Gray zone: "Menopause weight gain is real — here's a program built for this stage of life" (acknowledging) likely defensible; "stop menopause weight gain" is a treatment claim.

# FiftyStrong — primitives, types and the database

_The canonical reference for what the product is made of, how it is typed, and how it
is stored. One document on purpose: the content model, the templates that fill a
woman's program, and the tables that hold it are three layers of one design, and a
reader who has only one layer misreads the others._

**Sources of truth, in order:** `src/content/types.ts` (content), `src/content/templates.ts`
(templates), `src/db/schema.ts` (storage), `drizzle/` (the migrations that build it).
This document explains what those files encode and why. Update it in the same commit
as any change to them — a reference that drifts is worse than none.

Companion: [`payments.md`](payments.md) for the access decision, the identifiers, and
the Stripe lifecycle. This document mentions `people` and `quiz_responses` only as far
as the program needs them.

Contents: the four layers · ① content · ② templates · ③ her program · ④ what she did ·
the other tables · runtime · what this replaced · deliberately absent · **the three
databases** · working with the schema.

---

## The four layers

```
① CONTENT (code)         Activity → GuidedWorkoutSession; Movement + GuidedWorkoutSessionMove → Move
                            │  referenced by slug — never copied into a row
② TEMPLATES (code)       ProgramTemplate → PeriodTemplate → ActivityDraft
                            │  expandPeriod + appendPeriod — read once, then let go
③ HER PROGRAM (rows)     person_programs → person_program_periods → person_program_activities
                            │  attempts.activity_id, nullable
④ WHAT SHE DID (rows)    attempts → attempt_moves · check_ins
```

Layers ① and ② live in TypeScript, versioned with the media they reference and
type-checked. Layers ③ and ④ are Postgres — Supabase in production, PGlite in tests.
The seam between the halves is an **id held as text** — `activity_id` on a planned
activity or an attempt, `move_slug` on a finished movement — naming something in the
code catalog, deliberately not a foreign key, because the thing it names is not in the
database.

Three ideas run through the whole thing:

- **Her rows are the program.** A template is read once, when somebody fills a period,
  and after that has no hold over her plan. Editing a template cannot reach a woman
  partway through. That is the property the old jsonb document bought by copying
  itself, obtained without the copy.
- **The plan is what we asked of her; the attempts are what she did.** Separate tables
  on purpose. The gap between them is the only honest measure of adherence.
- **Store the raw action, plus any context that cannot be reconstructed from it.**
  Percentages, counts, "where is she" and "did she abandon" are all derived. What is
  stored is the movement she finished and the version of the session she ran.

Typed declarative data. No table holds any of it.

**Why:** 82% of the ~470 women who finished the quiz in the last 60 days picked "lose weight,

the plan reveal and the paywall never mention it again. She tells us what she came for on
screen 4 and we answer a different question for the next 28 screens.

**What this is:** a screen-by-screen replacement for the live quiz that makes the middle the
spine of the funnel, borrowing the mechanics that make BetterMe's women's 28-question funnel
work, without its four tricks (BMI verdict, goal-weight projection, fabricated cohort numbers,
renewal trap). The movement assessment in Act 2 stays, because it is the only part that drives
the programme; everything around it is re-aimed.

**Position on "weight loss":** we sell the middle, not the scale. Science delivers the middle
(visceral fat about −6% with zero weight loss; waist −1.4 cm vs controls +2.0 cm in a 12-week
home RCT of 226 postmenopausal women) and barely moves the scale (−0.5 to −2 kg). Meta bans
weight-loss before/after imagery; the ASA banned a 12-week menopause programme for "rapid fat
loss". Her own words already split them: "it's not the weight gain, it's WHERE I'm gaining it."
So: no height, no weight, no goal weight, no BMI, no scale curve. Shape, clothes, firmness,
and her own tape measure instead.

## 4. Claims — what we can say on these screens

| Say | Never |
|---|---|
| "targets deep belly fat even when the scale barely moves" | "lose belly fat in 12 weeks" |
| "firmer through the middle", "clothes sit differently" | inches, pounds, kilos, % body fat, any number in a timeframe |
| "muscle is the lever; eating less alone takes muscle with it" | "boost your metabolism", "burn fat" |
| "your own waist measure, week 1 vs week 12" | a projected waist or weight curve |
| "menopause" inside the quiz, landing and email | "menopause belly" in any ad hook (memory + ad-research: ~0% of Reverse Health's long-running ads use the word) |
| "the rules changed", "it isn't willpower" | anything implying treatment of a symptom (ASA 12.1) |

Figures to verify before shipping: visceral share 5–8% → 15–20% (menopause-health-research
page); Verheggen 2016 −6%; the n=226 RCT waist figures (Bonsu 2025 per the brief); ½%/yr
muscle loss.

## 5. What this asks of the product

The programme is strength, balance and mobility at 3 × ~18 min. That is exactly the
intervention in the visceral-fat evidence, so the claims hold. Two things it owes the
middle-first woman:

1. **A visible walking strand.** The RCTs that moved waist combined resistance work with
   walking. A "walk on the days between" prompt in the week view costs nothing to build and
   makes the promise honest.
2. **The waist retest.** 4.6 stores a number; week 12 has to ask for it again and show both.
   Otherwise the one measurement we promised is the one we never revisit.

Neither blocks the quiz change. Both should ship before the arm gets real spend.

---

## 6. How to test it

Run as a fourth arm against the live quiz, same ads, same landing. Read in this order:

1. Screen-1 engagement (`quiz_screen_viewed` s1-1 → `quiz_started`) — the age door vs the stage door. Live: 50%.
2. Completion to paywall. Live: ~97% of starters who give an email.
3. `plan_selected` / `checkout_started` per paywall view. Live: 0 for 34 in the last diagnosis; 5.7% lead → InitiateCheckout on the older flow.
4. Drop-off at 1.8 (what have you tried) and 4.6 (waist) — the two screens most likely to cost completion.

Kill the arm if screen-1 engagement falls; keep it if checkout rate moves at all, because
nothing else in the live funnel has.

## 2. Scoring / results logic (client `window.FS`, mirrored server-side in `src/lib/prescription.ts`)

**Four axes:** `mobility`, `balance`, `strength`, `energy` (tie-break priority in that order).

**Inputs (0–1 quality per answer):**
- s2-2 floor, s2-3 stairs, s2-5 afternoon: `[1, .67, .33, 0]`
- s2-4 one-leg: `[1, .5, 0, null]` ("I've never tried" = missing data → axis marked *estimated*)
- s2-6 stiffness: "Nowhere much" = 1; otherwise `max(0, 1 − regions/4)`

**Weighted axis score (0–100):**
- mobility = s2-2 ×2 + s2-6 ×2
- balance = s2-4 ×2 + s2-2 ×1
- strength = s2-2 ×2 + s2-3 ×1
- energy = s2-3 ×2 + s2-5 ×2
- then + activity modifier (s2-1: −8 / −3 / +3 / +8) + age allowance (s1-3: 0 / 3 / 6 / 9 / 12), clamped 0–100.
- **Symptom nudge:** an s1-5 symptom mapped to an axis (stiff→mobility, energy dips→energy, sleep→energy, unsteady→balance, heavier→strength) subtracts 6 pts, but only if the measured score is < 55 ("measurement outranks self-report"); ≥ 55 it is marked *contradicted* and the bar says "…better than you flagged it".

**Levels:** < 35 "Needs attention" · < 55 "Room to build" · < 75 "Holding up" · else "Going well".

**Profile:** rank axes ascending; `primary` = lowest (what the plan leads with, "Start here"), `secondary` = next. Goal axis from s1-4: weight→null, steadier→balance, stronger→strength, stiffness→mobility, energy→energy. **Mode:** `none` (no goal) · `weight` (goal 0) · `confirm` (goal axis == primary) · `reconcile` (goal ≠ primary) · `maintain` (primary ≥ 75 overrides). Reconcile copy on s2-11: e.g. "You said you want to **{goal}**. Your answers say {goal axis} is holding up better than you'd think — it's {primary} making everything feel harder. {Primary} first gets you there faster." (variant when goal axis < 55: "…does need work — but {primary} is further behind, and it is holding {goal} back.").

**Guards** (s2-10 + s2-8>0 → pelvic floor) feed the "built around {your bones / your joint replacement / your back / your heart / your recovery / the dizziness / your pelvic floor}" line on the paywall and the server Prescription.

**Server Prescription** (`/api/quiz` save → `FSRX`, cached in `localStorage.fs_rx`): recomputes lead/sessionLead/outcomeEmphasis, an `arc {w34, w58, w912}`, intro line, 4 programme blocks, guards, bands (1–4 per axis). Client only renders it. Radar week-12 target = `min(92, score + 34)` per axis.

**Why.** 82% of the ~470 women who finished the quiz in the last 60 days picked "lose weight,
especially around my middle" as their one goal (PostHog `quiz_screen_submitted`, per-person
crosstab, `.claude/issue-funnels/issue-funnels-before-after.md` §8). In the live code that goal
maps to no scoring axis (`GOAL_AXIS[1] = null`, mode `weight`), so the diagnosis screen shows
"Primary goal: Lose weight, especially around my middle" directly above "Balance is where you
have the most to gain". She names what she came for on screen 5 and nothing in the next 27
screens mentions it again. The paywall converted 0 of 34 in the last diagnosis.

**What this is.** A screen-by-screen replacement that makes the middle the spine of the funnel,
borrowing the mechanics that make BetterMe's women's 28-question funnel work, and leaving out its
four tricks: the BMI verdict, the goal-weight projection, the fabricated cohort numbers and the
renewal trap. Act 2 (the movement assessment) stays almost untouched because it is the only part
that drives the programme; everything around it is re-aimed.

**Position on "weight loss".** We sell the middle, not the scale. The science delivers the
middle (visceral fat about −6% with zero weight loss, Verheggen 2016; waist −1.4 cm vs controls
+2.0 cm in a 12-week home RCT of 226 postmenopausal women) and barely moves the scale
(−0.5 to −2 kg). Meta bans weight-loss before/after imagery; the ASA banned a 12-week menopause
programme for "rapid fat loss". Her own words already separate the two: "it's not the weight
gain, it's WHERE I'm gaining it." So: no height, no weight, no goal weight, no BMI, no scale
curve. Shape, clothes, firmness, and her own tape measure instead.

## 1. What to take from BetterMe, and what to leave

| BetterMe mechanic | Take? | Our version |

## 5. What this asks of the product

The programme is strength, balance and mobility at 3 × ~15 min from a chair. That is the
intervention in the visceral-fat evidence, so the claims hold. Two things it owes a woman who
came for the middle:

1. **A visible walking strand.** The RCTs that moved waist paired resistance work with walking.
   A "walk on the days between" line in the week view is cheap and makes the promise honest.
2. **The waist retest.** 4.6 stores a number; the week-12 retest has to ask again and show both.
   The one measurement we promised cannot be the one we never revisit.

Neither blocks the quiz change. Both should ship before this arm gets real spend.

## 6. How to test it

Ship as a new arm beside the live quiz, same ads, same landing, hashed on `FSID` like the others.
Read in this order:

1. Screen-1 engagement (`quiz_screen_viewed` s1-1 → `quiz_started`): the age door against the stage door. Live: ~50%.
2. Completion to `paywall_viewed`. Live: ~97% of those who give an email.
3. `plan_selected` and `checkout_started` per paywall view. Live: 0 of 34 in the August diagnosis; 5.7% lead → InitiateCheckout on the older flow.
4. Drop-off at 1.8 and 4.6, the two screens most likely to cost completion.

Kill it if screen-1 engagement falls. Keep it if checkout rate moves at all, because nothing
else in the live funnel has.

Mechanics
Seven patterns worth naming, ordered by how much they matter.
The trial costs more than not having one
$14.99/mo to start immediately, $19.99/mo if you take the 7-day trial, and the immediate option is pre-selected. The trial is priced as a convenience fee for hesitation. Most competitors run this the other way — trial as the default, paid as the escape hatch — which makes this a deliberate and unusual call, and one worth watching rather than copying blind.
The ATT prompt is timed to the peak, not the launch
Push permission fires mid-quiz over a reassurance screen; the tracking prompt fires at the exact moment the plan resolves and the user's name appears on screen. Neither is at cold launch, where most apps put them and where they are most often refused.
Twenty-eight questions with a visible spine
Five named sections — About You, Habits, Nutrition, Motivation, Almost There — each with a segmented progress bar. The length is the point: it manufactures the sunk cost that makes the paywall survivable. Every question also carries a one-line rationale, which is what stops the length feeling extractive.
Diagnosis before prescription
The funnel does not just collect a weight, it returns a verdict on it — live BMI classification, then a full summary screen plotting you against “normal” with a named list of medical risks. The problem is established as clinical before the product is offered as the fix.
The projection is drawn to land early
Goal weight is projected for Dec 4 against a user-entered event of Dec 12. Whatever date you give it, the plan finishes comfortably before it.
No strength training anywhere in the funnel
The seven activity options are General Fitness, Wall Pilates, Pilates, Calisthenics, Walking, Stretching, Yoga. There is no weights, resistance, or strength option — and “Build Muscle” is offered as a goal two screens earlier. The App Store subtitle confirms the positioning: 
Pilates, calisthenics, yoga.
Two of twenty-eight answers stay editable
After purchase, 
Change preferences
 exposes exactly two screens: medical programs and activity types. Goal, target zone, body type, dream shape, pace and event date — the answers that did the emotional work in the funnel — are locked at purchase. The quiz is weighted toward converting you, not toward staying accurate about you.
The walking sessions are the only real programming
The fitness player is a flat sequence of 20-second intervals. The 
walking
 player is genuinely structured — Brisk Walking 7:00 alternating with Deep Breathing 2:00 across five phases — with a health notice covering warm-up, breathing rhythm and MHR training zones. The one place the product does progression, it does it well, which makes its absence everywhere else look like a choice.
The unit is a calorie target, not a session
“Do Your Workout” is really a 550 kcal daily burn goal, user-adjustable on a 400–700 wheel, fillable from the library or a custom entry. Sessions rotate day to day within the modalities the quiz fixed. That is a 
habit-completion
 model, not a training model.
The personalisation is real, and it is shallow
The quiz genuinely drives the plan: pick Walking and Wall Pilates and the day's activities come back as a Calorie Burn Hike and a Wall Pilates mobility session; say Belly and the workout's focus zone reads Belly. But it is 
selection, not programming
 — the quiz filters a fixed library into a daily list. There is no progression, no load, no periodisation. Every workout in a collection is 20–21 minutes and labelled Medium.
The plan is a checklist, not a program
“My Plan” is five daily tasks — mindset chapter, log calories, do your workout, weigh-in, drink water. The back arrow reaches previous days and retains them, but there is 
no forward view
: you cannot see the week ahead or what training builds toward. The unit of the product is 
a day
, not a block.
Most of the product is not the workout
The workout is one row of five. Behind the other four sit a full calorie tracker with AI photo logging and a 10,000-item database, a CBT-flavoured content track with narrated audio and sequential gating, a water tracker, and Apple Health integration. Judged on surface area this is a 
habit and nutrition app that also has workouts
.
Retention pressure runs all the way down
Exit-intent modals guard articles 
and
 audio; a reminder-scheduling prompt fires after the first food log; a review gate fires immediately after that, at the success moment. The same instinct that shaped the funnel is present in every corner of the product.
Rough edges in the paid experience
Weigh-in is hard-gated behind Apple Health with no skip, and on an unconfigured device it dead-ends in Apple's Health onboarding. The food database returns duplicates that disagree with each other. After paying, the account is still a 
guest
 — the subscription rides on the Apple ID with nothing to recover.
Adaptation runs on a single question
The only feedback channel is a post-workout three-point exertion scale — could do more / just right / ready to drop — explicitly labelled as shaping the next session. Cheap, well-placed, and the entire adaptive mechanism.
Paying is the start of the selling
Three upsell screens fire before the app opens. After that: a $21.99 challenge, a $29.99/12-week trainer behind the chat icon, a hardware store in the More tab, and merch inside the workout screen itself. Several collections in the library are built around kit they sell.
Time-based, equipment-light, no load
Every exercise is a 20-second interval with a video demo and no rep count, no weight, and no progression. For a general-fitness Pilates audience that is a defensible design. For anyone training strength it is a ceiling, and it is the same ceiling the quiz's missing strength option implies.
A hard wall, with no second chance
No close affordance, no back gesture, no exit-intent discount, and relaunching returns you to the same screen. Zero product surface is visible before payment — the entire evaluation is done on the strength of the quiz alone.
So what
For FiftyStrong
Five decisions this teardown puts on the table.
Their gap is your category, and the product confirms it
BetterMe has no strength training. Not a thin offering — none. The activity picker goes Pilates, calisthenics, yoga, walking, and the App Store subtitle says the same. They will still take a “Build Muscle” answer and route it into Pilates. Post-paywall this holds all the way down: every exercise is a 20-second timed interval with no reps, no weight and no progression, and much of the library is organised around Pilates kit they sell. For a strength product aimed at women, that is the whole opening.
Beat them on programming, not on content volume
Their plan is a 
daily checklist
, not a training block — and on day one neither date arrow moves, so a user cannot see the week ahead. Nothing progresses: every workout in a collection is 20–21 minutes and labelled Medium. A product that shows a real block, tracks load, and visibly gets harder is differentiated against this without needing a bigger library.
Copy the two-tap first workout
Past the upsells, they put a user into a 
4-minute, 7-exercise, no-equipment
 session before showing any navigation, then ask a single exertion question and schedule the next one. That sequence — tiny first ask, immediate feedback, commitment to a next date — is the strongest retention design in the app and the cheapest thing here to reproduce.
Steal the rationale, not the length
The thing that makes 28 questions tolerable is that each sensitive one carries a single line explaining why it is being asked, plus a “Sources of recommendations” link. That habit is cheap to copy and is most of the trust. The length itself is a cost they pay for sunk-cost pressure at the wall.
Decide your position on the diagnosis lever
Live BMI verdicts and a named list of medical risks are effective and are the most ethically loaded thing in this funnel. It is a real fork for FiftyStrong: an audience motivated by capability rather than pathology needs a different lever, and choosing not to run this one is a positioning decision, not an omission.
Permission timing is free conversion
Both prompts are placed at emotional highs rather than at launch. This costs nothing to implement and is likely worth several points of opt-in. Copy it directly.
Test showing something before the wall
Their bet is that zero free surface plus a long quiz beats a preview. It is a strong, defensible bet at their scale and brand recognition — 711k ratings, #46 in Health & Fitness. It is a much riskier bet for an unknown app, where a single completed workout may do more for conversion than another interstitial.

## 4. Guardrails, per mechanic

1. **Body figures (1.5, 1.6, P1, 6.4).** Illustrated, not photographic. Four "now" shapes × four
   "after" shapes × five age bands is 80 pairs; build 4 + 4 figures per age band (40 renders) and
   composite. The "after" is firmer and upright, same hair, same face, same clothes; never thin,
   never a decade younger. Meta prohibits weight-loss before/after imagery in ads and reviews
   landing pages; illustration plus a "typical results vary" line is the defensible form. Run P1
   as an A/B against the functional pair before it becomes the default.
2. **BMI (4.2, 6.2).** Show the number and band. No disease list. One line that it is blunt after
   50. The Sculpted Vegan ruling was about claims, not about showing a BMI; showing hers is fine.
3. **Weight timeline (4.3, 6.3, P3).** Rate 0.25–0.5 kg/week (CAP 13.10 cap is ~0.9 kg). The
   curve is drawn from her inputs at that rate; it is never bent to land before an event. If the
   event is too close, say what she would reach. No "lose X in N weeks" copy anywhere; the chart
   is her estimate with a stated rate. CAP 13.9 bans a stated amount in a stated period for
   prospective users; a computed estimate from her own inputs with the rate disclosed is the
   nearest defensible form, and it is what BetterMe, Noom and Reverse Health all ship. Legal
   review before launch.
4. **Pace (4.5).** "As fast as possible" becomes "as fast as is safe" with the cap stated. The
   moderate and fast paces assume eating to the plan; the FAQ says so.
5. **Event (4.6, 4.7).** Used on the trajectory only. No countdown, no "reserved for 09:57".
6. **Waist (4.4).** Stays optional. It is the number the programme most reliably moves, so the
   week-12 retest asks for it again and the trajectory draws it moving first.

Verify before shipping: visceral share 5–8% → 15–20%; Verheggen 2016 −6%; the n=226 RCT waist
figures; ½%/yr muscle loss; the 0.5 kg/week rate against NICE/NHS guidance.

1. **Figure renders.** 40 illustrations, one style, consistent face/hair per age band. Cheapest
   route is a single illustrator or a locked image model with a character sheet.
2. **A walking and eating strand.** The moderate and fast paces are not honest on 3 × 15 min
   alone. The week view needs "walk on the days between" and a one-page "eating to the plan"
   guide (protein, no diet). Without them the trajectory is a promise the product does not keep.
3. **Weight and waist check-ins.** Store 4.2 / 4.3 / 4.4; ask weight fortnightly and waist at
   week 12; redraw 6.3 against actuals. That is the part BetterMe does not do.

New arm beside the live quiz, hashed on `FSID`. Read: screen-1 engagement (age door vs stage
door), completion to paywall (watch 4.2 and 4.3 in particular), `checkout_started` per paywall

1. **Figure style.** Recommend illustrated renders in one house style over AI photos: they read as

3. **Hot flushes.** Cut.
4. **Testimonials.** Cut until real.

Why the quiz has to change

The leak is not the price. It is that the funnel answers a question she did not ask.

In the live code the weight goal maps to no scoring axis (GOAL_AXIS[1] = null, mode weight). The diagnosis screen shows Primary goal: Lose weight, especially around my middle directly above Balance is where you have the most to gain. The plan blocks are hips, back and the floor. The testimonials are the banister, the sneeze and the afternoon slump. She names what she came for on screen 5 and none of the next 27 screens returns to it. In the August diagnosis 33 of 34 paywall viewers scrolled past the plan cards and not one tapped.

Position, revised: the middle first, the scale second, both measured

The science delivers the middle and barely moves the scale: exercise cuts visceral fat about 6% with zero weight loss (Verheggen 2016, 117 studies); a 12-week home programme in 226 postmenopausal women moved waist −1.4 cm while controls gained 2.0 cm; the scale moved −0.5 to −2 kg. So the story stays the middle. But she thinks in kilos, and BetterMe's numbers block is the part of their funnel that makes the plan feel like hers. v2 asks for her height, weight and goal, shows her BMI, and draws a trajectory at a safe pace on her own numbers, with the waist line moving first.

The women who pick the middle carry the same functional stack as the women who don't: 47% cannot get off the floor unaided, 57% stiff in the lower back, 75% leak at least sometimes, 88% sleep badly. The middle is the ticket she buys with. The programme she needs is the one we already have. The job is to make the quiz say so.

Guardrails, per mechanic

Written to the ASA standard, which makes it US-safe too. Each of the five borrowed mechanics has one.

  1. Body figures (1.5, 1.6, 6.4, P1). Illustrated, not photographic. Four "now" and four "after" figures per age band, 40 renders, composited into pairs. The "after" is firmer and upright, same hair, face and clothes; never thin, never a decade younger. Meta prohibits weight-loss before/after imagery in ads and reviews landing pages; illustration plus a "typical results vary" line is the defensible form. Run P1 as an A/B against the functional pair before it becomes the default.
  2. BMI (4.2, 6.2). Show the number and the band. No disease list. One line that it is blunt after 50. The Sculpted Vegan ruling was about efficacy claims, not about showing someone her BMI.
  3. Weight timeline (4.3, 6.3, P3). Rate 0.25–0.5 kg a week. The curve is drawn from her inputs at that rate and never bent to land before an event; if the event is too close, the screen says what she would reach. No "lose X in N weeks" copy anywhere. CAP 13.9 bans a stated amount in a stated period for prospective users; a computed estimate from her own inputs with the rate disclosed is the nearest defensible form, and it is what BetterMe, Noom and Reverse Health ship. Legal review of the exact copy before spend.
  4. Pace (4.5). "As fast as possible" becomes "as fast as is safe", cap stated. Moderate and fast assume eating to the plan; the FAQ says so.
  5. Event (4.6, 4.7). Drawn on the trajectory only. No countdown, no "reserved for 09:57".
  6. Waist (4.4). Optional. It is the number the programme most reliably moves, so the week-12 retest asks again and the trajectory draws it moving first.

Say

  • "your BMI is 27.5, above the healthy range"
  • "at a steady pace, 7 kg is around 16–28 weeks"
  • "the waist moves before the scale does"
  • "firmer through the middle", "clothes sit differently"
  • "menopause" inside the quiz, the landing page and email

Never

  • "lose 7 kg in 12 weeks", or any amount in a period as a promise
  • a disease list under the BMI
  • a curve that lands before her event
  • "boost your metabolism", "burn fat", "melt"
  • "menopause belly" in any ad hook

Verify before shipping: the visceral share 5–8% → 15–20%; Verheggen 2016, −6%; the n=226 RCT waist figures; the half-percent-a-year muscle loss; the 0.5 kg a week rate against NHS guidance.

What this asks of the product

The trajectory is a promise the product has to keep. Three things the numbers act creates.

  1. Figure renders. Forty illustrations in one house style with a consistent face and hair per age band. Cheapest route is one illustrator, or a locked image model with a character sheet.
  2. A walking and eating strand. The moderate and fast paces are not honest on three fifteen-minute sessions alone. The week view needs "walk on the days between" and a one-page "eating to the plan" guide. Without them the trajectory outruns the programme.
  3. Weight and waist check-ins. Store 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4; ask weight fortnightly and waist at week 12; redraw the trajectory against actuals. That is the part BetterMe does not do.

How to test it

Ship as a new arm beside the live quiz, same ads, same landing, hashed on the funnel id like the pricing and intro arms.

  1. Screen-1 engagement: the age door against the stage door. Live: about 50%.
  2. Completion to the paywall, watching 4.2 and 4.3 in particular. Live: about 97% of those who give an email.
  3. Checkout started per paywall view. Live: 0 of 34 in the August diagnosis.
  4. Inside the arm, A/B P1: her body pair against the functional photo pair.

Four decisions

Each has a recommendation. Say the word and the rest is build.

1

Figure style

Recommend illustrated renders in one house style over AI photos. They read as "a body like mine" rather than "a model", they sidestep identity drift, and they are the form Meta's landing-page review is least likely to flag.

2

Timeline legal review

Recommend shipping 6.3 as specified and getting a one-hour review of the exact copy before spend. It is the single highest-value and highest-risk screen in the funnel.

3

Hot flushes

Recommend cutting. The answer drives nothing, and 1.8 does the recognition job.

4

Testimonials

Recommend cutting until real ones exist. A middle-first page with banister quotes is worse than none.

- **Pace, secondary goals, event, date** are 4.5, 1.4, 4.6, 4.7. They drive 6.3, "Your trajectory": a dated weight curve at her chosen pace with the event as a marker, plus a waist line that moves first.
- **Paywall before/after** is P1, and the Now → Week 12 table under it gains weight, BMI and waist rows from her numbers.

The quiz grows to 44 screens and 27 inputs, against 32 and 18 live and BetterMe's 28 questions. A 39-screen lean cut is listed.

**Two guardrails I attached rather than argued against.** The trajectory is computed from her own numbers at 0.25 to 0.5 kg a week and never bent to land before her event; if the event is too close, the screen says how far she would get. The figures are illustrations, not photos, with the "after" firmer and upright rather than thin. Meta reviews landing pages for weight-loss imagery, so P1 should run as an A/B against the functional photo pair first. Both are written up in the Guardrails section, and the trajectory copy is the one screen I would put in front of a lawyer for an hour before spend.

**Product debts this creates.** Forty figure renders in one house style, a walking and eating strand so the moderate and fast paces are honest, and fortnightly weight plus week-12 waist check-ins so the trajectory can be redrawn against actuals.

Written to the ASA standard, which makes it US-safe too.

  1. Body figures (1.5, 1.6, 6.4, P1). Illustrated, not photographic. Four "now" and four "after" figures per age band, 40 renders, composited into pairs. Meta prohibits weight-loss before/after imagery in ads and reviews landing pages; illustration plus a "typical results vary" line is the defensible form.   2. BMI (4.2, 6.2). Show the number and the band. No disease list. One line that it is blunt after 50.

50Queen · belly quiz branch · v3 · 4 September 2026

The middle-first quiz

A branch of the main quiz for the 82% who pick the middle as their goal. It opens on the goal echo, takes her shape now and the shape she wants, keeps a short energy-and-activeness check, asks her numbers and shows her a BMI profile, surfaces the time and motivation worries and answers them with a with/without chart, sets the pace with BetterMe's 033 to 037 block, and lands on a paywall that opens with her own before/after. Every screen sits beside the BetterMe screen it takes after.

6interstitials, two of them charts

Where the branch starts

The main quiz keeps its door, its age and stage screens and the goal question. Answering "lose the weight around my middle" routes into this branch; the other four goals continue on the live flow.

In the live code the weight goal maps to no scoring axis, so the diagnosis screen shows Primary goal: Lose weight, especially around my middle above Balance is where you have the most to gain. She names what she came for and nothing after it returns to it. In the August diagnosis 33 of 34 paywall viewers scrolled past the plan cards and not one tapped. The branch exists to make every screen after the goal about the goal.

Position: the middle first, the scale measured

Exercise cuts visceral fat about 6% with zero weight loss (Verheggen 2016); a 12-week home programme in 226 postmenopausal women moved waist −1.4 cm vs +2.0 cm in controls; the scale moved −0.5 to −2 kg. So the story is the middle, and the numbers block gives her the kilos she thinks in: her weight, her goal, her BMI, a trajectory at a safe pace from her own inputs.

Guardrails

Written to the ASA standard, which makes it US-safe too.

  1. Body figures (1.2, 1.3, 3.4, P1). Illustrated, not photographic. Four "now" and four "after" figures per age band, 40 renders, composited into pairs. The "after" is firmer and upright, same hair, face and clothes; never thin, never a decade younger. Meta prohibits weight-loss before/after imagery in ads and reviews landing pages; illustration plus a "typical results vary" line is the defensible form. A/B P1 against the functional pair before it becomes the default.
  2. BMI (3.2, 3.4). The number and the band. No disease list. One line that it is blunt after 50.
  3. Weight charts (4.4, 5.5, P1). Rate 0.25–0.5 kg a week from her inputs. The curve is never bent to land before an event; if the event is too close the screen says what she would reach. The "without" line on 4.4 is sourced (average mid-life gain), not drawn for effect. No "lose X in N weeks" copy anywhere. CAP 13.9 bans a stated amount in a stated period; a computed estimate from her own inputs with the rate disclosed is the nearest defensible form, and it is what BetterMe, Noom and Reverse Health ship. Legal review of the exact copy before spend.
  4. Pace (5.1). "As fast as possible" becomes "as fast as is safe", cap stated. Moderate and fast assume eating to the plan; the FAQ says so.
  5. Event (5.3, 5.4). Drawn on the trajectory only. No countdown.

Say

  • "your BMI is 27.5, above the healthy range"
  • "at a steady pace, 7 kg is around 16–28 weeks"
  • "the waist moves before the scale does"
  • "firmer through the middle", "clothes sit differently"

Never

  • "lose 7 kg in 12 weeks", or any amount in a period as a promise
  • a disease list under the BMI
  • a curve that lands before her event
  • "boost your metabolism", "burn fat", "melt"
  • "menopause belly" in any ad hook

What this asks of the product

Three things the branch creates.

  1. Figure renders. Forty illustrations in one house style with a consistent face and hair per age band.
  2. The movement checks move in-app. Floor, stairs and one-leg are no longer in the quiz, so strength and balance are unmeasured at sign-up. Weight mode defaults to the strength block; the week-2 retest in the app measures the three items and picks the week-5 block. The scoring code needs a "quiz-partial" mode.
  3. A walking and eating strand, and check-ins. Moderate and fast paces are not honest on three fifteen-minute sessions alone; the week view needs "walk on the days between" and a one-page eating guide. Weight fortnightly, waist at week 12, trajectory redrawn against actuals.

Three decisions

Each has a recommendation.

1

Figure style

Recommend illustrated renders in one house style over AI photos. They read as "a body like mine", sidestep identity drift, and are the form Meta's landing-page review is least likely to flag.

2

Charts legal review

Recommend a one-hour review of the exact copy on 4.4, 5.5 and P1 before spend. They are the highest-value and highest-risk screens in the funnel.

3

The dropped movement checks

Recommend accepting the trade and measuring in-app at week 2. The quiz gets shorter and stays on the goal; the cost is that the first two weeks are the fixed on-ramp for everyone anyway, so nothing is lost before the retest.

Reference screens: BetterMe women's app onboarding (captured on device, August 2026) and BetterMe web funnel 4845 (men's calisthenics, 248px, so small type is soft). Sources: PostHog quiz_screen_submitted crosstab · audience brief §6–8 · live quiz on lead-rate-experiments. Working document, not for distribution.

# Feature: quiz-email-capture

## User Story

As a woman taking the quiz, I give my email right after my name so my plan, my sign-in link, and my checkout are already addressed to me — and as the operator, every record of her (quiz sitting, person, Stripe customer, analytics identity) carries the same email so the funnel joins on it.

## User Flow

1. She reaches s4-4 ("What should we call you?"), types her name.
2. An email field sits directly below the name field. She types her email; Continue advances only once the email looks valid.
3. The sitting saves as before — now carrying `email` — so `quiz_responses.email` is set.
4. Analytics pick it up at capture: PostHog identifies her (person gets `$email`), Meta pixel re-inits with advanced matching (`em`), an `email_captured` event fires (no raw email in event properties).
5. At the paywall she taps Start my plan → `/api/checkout` looks up her sitting and passes `customer_email`, so Stripe Checkout opens with her email prefilled.
6. She pays. Provisioning sets `people.email` from the Stripe session as today; if Stripe somehow carries no email, it falls back to the sitting's email.

## Success Criteria

- [x] SC1: Email field renders directly below the name field on s4-4 (`type=email`, `autocomplete=email`, `inputmode=email`), and Continue on s4-4 is gated on a syntactically valid email (name stays optional). — **Verify by:** browser E2E on the running app: screenshot of s4-4; Continue with empty/invalid email stays on s4-4 with inline hint; valid email advances.
- [x] SC2: The client save carries email and `quiz_responses.email` is persisted with no-clobber semantics; `/api/quiz` validates it (trimmed, ≤254 chars, must look like an email or stored as null). — **Verify by:** new unit tests in `src/db/quiz.email.test.ts` (or extended existing suite) + route-level test; browser E2E: inspect POST `/api/quiz` body.
- [x] SC3: `/api/checkout` passes `customer_email` from the sitting when there is no returning Stripe customer, and omits it when `returning.stripeCustomerId` is present (Stripe rejects `customer` + `customer_email` together). — **Verify by:** unit test with mocked Stripe capturing `sessions.create` params, both branches.
- [x] SC4: Stripe Checkout opens with the email prefilled. — **Verify by:** browser E2E in Stripe test mode from the paywall; screenshot of the Checkout page showing the email.
- [x] SC5: Provisioning falls back to the sitting's email when the Stripe session has none, so `people.email` is never null for a converter who gave one. — **Verify by:** unit test on the provisioning path (`createPersonFromQuiz` / `fulfil` details) with a session lacking email.
- [x] SC6: PostHog: at capture, `FSPH.identify()` sets `$email` (and `name`) on the person — a documented, scoped exemption from the redactor — and an `email_captured` event fires with no raw email in event properties; the shared event catalogue test passes. — **Verify by:** `pnpm test` (events/static-analytics/redact suites) + browser E2E with `?dev=1` console showing the `[posthog]` lines.
- [x] SC7: Meta pixel re-inits with advanced matching (`fbq('init', ID, {em})`) once the email is captured. — **Verify by:** browser E2E with `?dev=1`: console/pixel log line; static test asserting the code path exists in the built page.
- [x] SC8: `static-src/quiz/index.html` is the edited source and `pnpm sync-static-pages` regenerates `quiz.ts`/`analytics.ts` with only the intended diff (source and bundle cannot drift). — **Verify by:** run the sync; `git diff --stat`; existing `static-analytics.test.ts` green.
- [x] SC9: Full suite green: `pnpm test`. — **Verify by:** test run output recorded.

## Platform & Stack

- **Platform:** Web (Next.js App Router + hand-authored static quiz page)
- **Language:** TypeScript (server), vanilla JS inside the static page
- **Key pieces:** `web/static-src/quiz/index.html` (+ `static-src/analytics.js`) → `pnpm sync-static-pages` → `src/static-pages/*.ts`; Drizzle/Postgres; Stripe Checkout; PostHog via first-party `/ingest`; Meta pixel.

## Steps to Verify

1. `cd web && pnpm test` — all suites.
2. `pnpm sync-static-pages` then `git diff` — only intended changes.
3. `pnpm dev` → `http://localhost:3000/quiz?dev=1` → walk to s4-4 → verify field, gating, POST body, console analytics lines.
4. Continue to `#s5-5` → Start my plan → Stripe test-mode Checkout shows the email prefilled.

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1: Server thread

- Scope: `/api/quiz` email validation; `/api/checkout` sitting lookup → `customer_email`; provisioning fallback (quiz email when session has none); update the stale provenance comment on `people.email` in `schema.ts`; update `web/docs/payments.md` identifiers/plans prose touching email in the same commit.
- Success criteria covered: SC2 (server half), SC3, SC5
- Verification gate: new + existing unit/integration tests green.

### Phase 2: Page + analytics

- Scope: s4-4 email field + Continue gating + restore-on-reload (match whatever the name field does); `FSQuiz.send()` carries email; `static-src/analytics.js`: `FSPH.identify()` (scoped `$email` exemption, documented), `email_captured` in the shared catalogue, `FSTrack.setEmail()` advanced-matching re-init; regenerate via `pnpm sync-static-pages`.
- Success criteria covered: SC1, SC2 (client half), SC6, SC7, SC8
- Verification gate: catalogue/redact/static tests green; dev-mode browser walkthrough.

### Phase 3: End-to-end + audit

- Scope: full funnel run in the browser with Stripe test mode; evidence capture; independent `verification-auditor` run.
- Success criteria covered: SC4, SC9 (+ re-confirm SC1/SC2/SC6/SC7 live)
- Verification gate: auditor PASS.

## Decision Log

- **Email placement: same screen as the name (s4-4), field directly below.** Eugene: "the email field should be right after the name." One-question-per-screen grammar bends rather than breaks: name+email are one identity moment, and BetterMe also pairs capture with the reveal boundary.
- **Email is required to continue past s4-4.** "Collect the email" is the point; an optional field collects a fraction. Gentle inline copy, no red shouting. Name stays optional as today.
- **Microcopy under the field:** "Your plan and your sign-in link land here. Nothing else — no newsletter." — consistent with the page's promise style.
- **PostHog gets `$email` via a new `identify()` path, not by weakening the redactor.** The scrub still redacts email-shaped strings from all event properties; the exemption is only the person-property set inside `identify`, documented inline. `person_profiles: 'identified_only'` means this is also the moment she gains a person profile — which is exactly right: she stops being anonymous when she tells us who she is.
- **Meta advanced matching: yes, email only.** The page's existing privacy stance (never send the archetype/health inference to Meta) is untouched; `em` is standard advanced matching on a first-party conversion funnel and materially improves attribution. Flagging here for Eugene's async review.
- **`people.email` provenance: Stripe session first, quiz sitting as fallback.** The Stripe email is payment-verified and she confirmed it at Checkout (prefilled from the quiz anyway); the sitting's email only fills a gap, never overrides.
- **Store email trimmed, original case, ≤254 chars; reject-to-null on shape failure** rather than 400 — a malformed email must not lose her sitting save (same tolerance philosophy as the answers path). Verified live: posting a sitting with `"not-an-address"` kept both answers and returned 200, and a later save with a valid address filled it in.
- **Enter on the name field now moves focus to the email field instead of advancing the screen.** Advancing straight past an empty required field would immediately bounce her back with an error; moving focus is the behaviour a two-field form should have. Enter on the email field commits and advances.
- **The error message distinguishes empty from malformed** ("We need an address to send your plan to." vs "That does not look like an email address — could you check it?"). One generic message for both makes a typo look like a refusal to accept her address at all.
- **Validation fires on leaving the screen, never while typing**, and the error clears on the next keystroke — nothing is marked wrong mid-address.
